h1: Futuristic Shenzhen Shows Trump the Difficulty of Stopping China
category: 美国《彭博社》外刊讲解 第1236天
nav_hint: 深圳科技：从山寨到未来之城

paragraphs.en_html: Under the towering skyscrapers home to some of China's biggest tech giants, a small group of foreigners tilt up their smartphones to capture a drone descending from the Shenzhen sky with a fresh serving of bubble tea. They’ve paid around $90 a head to be dazzled by the southern Chinese city's tech wonders on a tour led by Sean Zhang, who returned home in 2023 after studying in California. He's now cashing in as tourists flock to Shenzhen to experience frontier technologies like flying robotaxis, wearable exoskeletons and buildings shaped like giant AirPods. Influencers on Western social media platforms regularly post videos with titles like “China built a city that feels like 2050!” “Shenzhen usually leaves a very good impression,” says Zhang, 27, who has more than doubled the number of tours offered over the past year. “Many walk away saying: ‘This isn’t what I expected of China.’”

At the turn of the century, Shenzhen was best known for its cheap knock-offs of Western goods. Today, the city's progress serves as a powerful symbol of China's technological rise. BYD Co. last year dethroned US giant Tesla Inc. as the world's top supplier of electric vehicles, while SZ DJI Technology Co. now controls about 70% of the global consumer drone market. Shenzhen saw the highest population growth rate of any major Chinese city last year, and has one of the country's youngest average urban populations at 32.5 years old. Airport signs declare: “Once Here Shenzhener Forever.”

Shenzhen is among several megacities competing to be China's version of Silicon Valley. Beijing's top colleges produce some of the brightest AI researchers working at leading labs like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI. Shanghai and neighboring Hangzhou — home to Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. — are better known for fast-to-market AI applications for global markets. Shenzhen stands out for its supply chains that help AI integrate into everyday life.

One company emblematic of that strength is Seeed Studio, which focuses on “physical AI” — sensors, cameras and robot arms connecting AI to real-world tasks. Its studio displays warehouse interfaces, a chicken-farm system, panda conservation sensors and an AI-and-inventor van touring rural areas. “But I think after five years post-Covid, we have much stronger confidence and trust.”

Inside the souvenir shop at Huawei's headquarters, some of founder Ren Zhengfei's favorite phrases appear on the merchandise. “Victory is our belief and persistence is the only way out,” reads a box of fridge magnets, which are molded into the shape of Heidelberg Castle, a replica of which is featured at one of the company's campuses. Huawei's sprawling, tree-lined headquarters sits less than an hour's drive from the APEC venue. At the grand Darwin Hall, a giant graphic declared: “Huawei Business Growth Back on Track.” Of roughly 213,000 total employees, more than 53% are now engaged in research and development.

One testament to that shift is Huaqiangbei, described as the world's largest electronics marketplace. Ryan, a 25-year-old Shenzhen native who studied in Europe, remembers visiting the area as a child with his father. Now looking more like Tokyo's Akihabara Electric Town, it's transformed from a drab secondhand-electronics hub into a neon-lit mall with Chinese-branded drones, robotic dogs and droves of foreign visitors. Many come from Hong Kong, attracted by the city's wide spaces and cheap prices — a reversal from a few years ago, when mainlanders flocked to the former British colony.

Shenzhen produces nearly 8 million service robots, or 43% of last year's national output. Kevin Zhou, author of a Chinese biography of OpenAI's Sam Altman, said Shenzhen must focus on capturing the opportunity in embodied AI and avoid simply assembling the hardware while others control the underlying technology and capture the profits. “As models get cheaper and more open, value will shift to whoever can put them into robots and devices at scale,” he said. “And no city is better placed for that than Shenzhen.”

A new generation of entrepreneurs is looking to navigate the more fractured geopolitical landscape and become world leaders in their fields. Among them is Will Wang, a former Apple Inc. engineer who founded AI smart-glasses maker Even Realities in 2023. The startup reached a $1 billion valuation after raising $150 million in a funding round led by Meituan, with participation from Tencent. His ambition is to build a premium global brand, starting with developed markets before expanding into China. “You absolutely have to be the defining force of your category,” he said at his minimalist office in Shenzhen along an avenue of gleaming glass towers where hardware startups, robotics teams and AI developers operate side-by-side.

Livra, a 30-year-old who moved to Shenzhen from central China a decade ago, has a startup supplying batteries for drones and robotics across the US, Middle East and Europe. On the Shenzhen technology tour with Zhang, the bubble tea delivery softly touched down, drawing coos of excitement. Zhang pointed to the steady emergence of new shopping malls around town as evidence that standing still isn’t an option in Shenzhen. “It's like that in tech, too,” he said. “If you’re not at the forefront, then you’ll be left behind.”
